Yash: You started in March too, right? Same level as me?
Hansa: Yes. Level two.
Yash: What did they offer you? I only ask because I found out they told me a lot more than I expected.
Hansa: I didn't ask. They phoned on Friday and I said yes before they'd finished the sentence. I thought if I hesitated it would disappear.
Yash: Nothing at all? Not one question?
Hansa: Not one. I could have asked about a joining bonus, or a review. I keep thinking about that.
Yash: Mine is quite a bit more than you told me yours is.
Hansa: I know. I saw the pay slip mix-up. It stung.
Yash: It's done. But next time, ask one thing. Only one.
Hansa: One. Okay.

qa.a: The company phoned Hansa on Friday.

qa.q: What is Hansa feeling now about accepting so fast?
qa.a: Hansa feels regret and a sting, thinking that even one question should have been asked.

qa.q: What could Hansa do next time, and why?
qa.a: Hansa could ask one clear question, such as about a joining bonus or a review, because asking rarely makes an offer vanish and can improve it.

qa.q: How might Yash feel about telling Hansa?
qa.a: Yash probably feels awkward and sympathetic, wanting to help Hansa learn from it rather than feel worse.

grounding: Illustrates accepting the first offer at once for fear of losing it, then learning colleagues at the same level were paid more and regretting not asking.

subtype: Approach: accepting the first offer from fear of losing it [Pitfall]
passage:
Two years ago, the phone rang while I was on the metro and a voice said, "We'd like to offer you the analyst role." I said "Yes!" before she even finished the number.
I remember thinking, if I pause, they'll give it to someone else. My hands were shaking. I didn't ask about the salary, the review cycle, anything.
Last month, over lunch, Gopika mentioned her pay. She'd joined at the same level, three months after me. Her number was noticeably higher. So was Ravi's. They'd both asked one simple question: "Is there any flexibility?"
I didn't sleep well that night. Not because they did anything wrong. Because I never even tried.
Next time, I'll say "Thank you, can I take a day to look at it?" That's all it would have taken.
— Charu

qa.q: Where was Charu when the offer call came?
What was Charu afraid of when saying yes so quickly?
qa.a: Charu was afraid that pausing would make the company give the job to someone else, and was anxious enough that Charu's hands were shaking.

qa.q: What else could Charu have done on that call?
qa.a: Charu could have thanked them and asked for a day to consider, or asked whether there was any flexibility, instead of accepting at once.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel after learning what happened to Charu?
qa.a: Gopika may feel sympathetic and a little awkward, since sharing her pay showed Charu the gap without meaning to hurt.

grounding: It shows someone accepting the first offer out of fear of losing it, then learning peers at the same level were paid more and regretting not asking a question.

subtype: Approach: accepting the first offer from fear of losing it [Pitfall]
passage:
Career mentor's note — Women in Tech mentoring circle, Kochi

Ganga came to our session in March upset. I'm writing down what I saw so I remember it for the next group.
Six months ago, she received an offer for a QA engineer post. She told me the recruiter said, "Can you confirm today?" and she said yes within minutes, sure that hesitating would lose the job.
In March, Rekha, another tester from the same batch, joined the circle. Comparing notes over coffee, they found Rekha earned clearly more for the same role. Rekha had simply asked if the number could move.
Ganga kept saying, "I didn't ask one question." She looked more embarrassed than angry.
What I did next: we spent the session practising two lines for her upcoming review: asking what the band is, and asking what it would take to move within it.

qa.q: What did the recruiter ask Ganga?
qa.a: The recruiter said, "Can you confirm today?"

qa.q: How was Ganga feeling in the March session?
qa.a: Ganga was upset and looked more embarrassed than angry, full of regret at not asking even one question.

qa.q: What else could Ganga have done when asked to confirm the same day?
qa.a: She could have thanked the recruiter and asked whether there was any room on the number, or asked for a day to decide.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel after the pay comparison?
qa.a: Rekha may feel uncomfortable and sympathetic, since sharing Rekha's pay upset Ganga, though Rekha did nothing wrong by asking.

grounding: It shows, through a mentor's note, someone who accepted an offer at once from fear of losing it and later regretted not asking once she learned a peer was paid more.
